title: Is minimum-color cycle solvable in polynomial time under ETH?
formal: Assuming the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) specified below, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,c≥1 such that, for every explicitly edge-colored finite simple undirected graph G, A finds a simple cycle using the fewest distinct colors, or correctly reports that G is acyclic, within C(L+1)^c bit operations, where L is the total input length?
definitions: The graph has vertices 1,...,n, with n≥1. Its explicit encoding lists n and m=|E(G)| in binary, followed by the m distinct unordered endpoint pairs and a color κ(e)∈{1,...,max(1,m)} for every edge, all in binary with delimiters. The coloring need not be proper. A simple cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices v_1,...,v_t, with t≥3, whose consecutive pairs and {v_t,v_1} are edges. Its cost is the cardinality of {κ(e):e lies on the cycle}. The output is such a vertex sequence attaining the minimum cost, or an acyclic marker if no cycle exists. L includes every endpoint and color label, rather than an oracle for an arbitrary set function. Here ETH asserts that there is ε>0 for which no deterministic algorithm decides satisfiability of all 3-CNF formulas with N variables in time 2^(εN) times a polynomial in their binary encoding length. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses with at most three Boolean literals. This hypothesis is part of the mathematical setting of the target.
answer_criterion: Working under the stated ETH hypothesis, prove that the required polynomial-time algorithm exists or prove that none exists. An unconditional algorithm with correctness and polynomial bit-cost proof answers positively. A proof that any such algorithm would contradict ETH answers negatively. An obstruction relying only on a stronger unlisted hardness conjecture does not settle this target. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full conditional statement.
why: Locate the polynomial-time boundary for a simple explicit graph optimization problem with a quasipolynomial general algorithm.

importance.reason: A concise and distinctive optimization problem separating explicit color costs from the broader submodular-oracle setting.

progress.text: Fomin and coauthors give a quasipolynomial algorithm for cycles with monotone submodular costs, including the number of distinct colors.
Korhonen continues to ask for a polynomial algorithm or a complexity-theoretic obstruction for explicitly colored graphs.

context_blocks.text: Cycle length counts edges, while this cost counts distinct labels. A cycle can repeat the same color on many edges without increasing its cost, so the objective differs from ordinary shortest-cycle problems.

The number of colors in an edge set is a monotone submodular cost. The general submodular-cycle algorithm gives a quasipolynomial upper bound for this explicitly represented problem. Query lower bounds against arbitrary value oracles do not imply a time lower bound for these color labels.

The source explicitly permits an ETH-based negative answer. Accordingly ETH is stated as a standing hypothesis, fixing which conditional obstruction counts. The computational goal remains exact polynomial-time optimization on every explicit graph.

sentences: Each edge of an undirected graph carries a color label.
The objective is to find a simple cycle using as few different colors as possible.
A general quasipolynomial algorithm is known, but a polynomial bound remains unresolved.
The card fixes ETH as the standing hypothesis so that an ETH-based obstruction is a precise negative answer.
Explicit color input distinguishes this target from lower bounds for arbitrary submodular value oracles.
